title: Bradycardia with a pulse (adult)
subject: emergency
summary: Treat bradycardia (usually below 50/min) urgently only when it causes cardiopulmonary compromise: support ABC, look for causes, give atropine 1 mg IV (repeat to 3 mg), then transcutaneous pacing or an adrenaline or dopamine infusion, and arrange transvenous pacing early for high-risk blocks.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Clinically significant bradyarrhythmia: heart rate typically below 50/min and inappropriate for the clinical condition.
Cardiopulmonary compromise: hypotension or signs of shock, acutely altered mental status or syncope, ischaemic chest discomfort, acute heart failure.
High risk of asystole: Mobitz type II block, complete heart block with broad QRS, recent asystole or ventricular pauses over 3 seconds. Plan pacing even if currently stable.

Causes: inferior MI or ischaemia, drugs (beta blockers, calcium channel blockers, digoxin, amiodarone, ivabradine), hyperkalaemia, hypoxia, hypothermia, hypothyroidism, raised intracranial pressure, vasovagal.
India: consider organophosphate or carbamate poisoning, yellow oleander (Thevetia) seed ingestion and hyperkalaemia in CKD.

sections.title: Immediate steps
items: Airway, oxygen if hypoxaemic, assist ventilation if needed; hypoxia is a common reversible cause.
Cardiac monitor, BP and SpO2; apply pacing-capable defibrillator pads early in unstable patients; IV access; 12-lead ECG.
Stable without compromise: identify and treat the cause, monitor and observe; no chronotropic drug is needed.

sections.title: Investigations
items: 12-lead ECG: type of block, QRS width, ischaemia or infarction, signs of hyperkalaemia or digoxin effect.
Potassium, calcium, magnesium, glucose, renal function, troponin, blood gas, TSH; digoxin level if on digoxin; cholinesterase activity if organophosphate poisoning is suspected.
Review all medicines, including eye drops (timolol) and recent dose changes.

sections.title: Drugs and pacing (unstable)
items: Atropine 1 mg IV bolus, repeat every 3 to 5 minutes to a maximum of 3 mg (AHA 2025). ERC/RCUK use 500 micrograms, repeated to a total of 3 mg.

Atropine is ineffective and may worsen block in high-degree AV block with broad QRS; do not give it to heart transplant recipients (risk of sinus arrest or high-grade block). Go straight to pacing or an infusion.

If atropine fails: transcutaneous pacing and/or adrenaline infusion 2 to 10 micrograms/min or dopamine infusion 5 to 20 micrograms/kg/min, titrated to response. ERC also lists isoprenaline starting at 5 micrograms/min.

Transcutaneous pacing: demand mode, set a rate of about 60/min, increase current until electrical capture, confirm mechanical capture by a femoral pulse or arterial trace, and give analgesia and sedation.
Arrange transvenous pacing early (cardiology) for persistent unstable bradycardia, Mobitz II or complete heart block; transcutaneous pacing is only a bridge.
Heart transplant or spinal cord injury: aminophylline 100 to 200 mg by slow IV injection (ERC).

sections.title: Cause-specific treatment
items: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes: 10 mL of 10% calcium chloride IV over 5 minutes (or 30 mL of 10% calcium gluconate over 10 minutes), then insulin-glucose and definitive potassium removal.
Beta blocker or calcium channel blocker toxicity: consider glucagon, IV calcium and high-dose insulin euglycaemia therapy with toxicology advice.

Organophosphate poisoning: atropine 1.8 to 3 mg IV, doubling the dose every 5 minutes until the chest is clear, heart rate above 80/min and systolic BP above 80 mmHg; follow the OP poisoning protocol.
Digoxin toxicity with life-threatening bradyarrhythmia: digoxin-specific antibody fragments where available; correct potassium and magnesium.
Inferior MI: AV block is often vagal and responds to atropine; treat the infarct with reperfusion. AV block with anterior MI implies extensive infarction and usually needs pacing.

sections.title: Disposition
items: Admit to a monitored bed (CCU) any symptomatic bradycardia, Mobitz II, complete heart block, or bradycardia needing drugs or pacing.
Refer to cardiology for permanent pacing assessment once reversible causes (drugs, ischaemia, electrolytes, hypothyroidism) are excluded or treated.
Stop or reduce rate-slowing drugs; watch for recurrence as drug effects wear off.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Repeating atropine in broad-complex complete heart block instead of pacing.
Accepting electrical artefact as capture during transcutaneous pacing without checking for a pulse.
Missing hyperkalaemia (renal failure, ACE inhibitors, spironolactone) or drug toxicity as the cause.
Treating asymptomatic physiological bradycardia (athletes, sleep).

drugs.name: Atropine
drugs.dose: 1 mg IV bolus every 3 to 5 minutes, maximum total 3 mg (AHA 2025); ERC 500 micrograms IV repeated to 3 mg
drugs.notes: Not for heart transplant recipients; ineffective in broad-complex high-degree AV block.

drugs.name: Adrenaline (epinephrine) infusion
drugs.dose: 2 to 10 micrograms/min IV, titrated to response
drugs.notes: Example: 1 mg in 50 mL (20 micrograms/mL) runs at 6 to 30 mL/h for 2 to 10 micrograms/min.

drugs.name: Dopamine infusion
drugs.dose: 5 to 20 micrograms/kg/min IV, titrated to response; taper slowly
drugs.notes: Alternative to adrenaline when atropine fails.

drugs.name: Isoprenaline infusion
drugs.dose: Start 5 micrograms/min IV, titrate to response

drugs.name: Aminophylline
drugs.notes: Bradycardia after heart transplant or spinal cord injury (ERC).

drugs.name: Calcium chloride 10%
drugs.dose: 10 mL IV over 5 minutes (or calcium gluconate 10%, 30 mL over 10 minutes)
drugs.notes: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes; calcium channel blocker toxicity.
